Luang Pu Thuad is among the most revered monks in Thailand, regarded with Somdej Toh as one of the country’s two great masters. Honoured especially in the south, he is revered too by Chinese Buddhists in Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia, and pilgrims cross the border to his temples. Great statues of him stand across Thailand, and stupas and temples, some in Malaysia, are said to mark where his body rested on its way back to Wat Chang Hai.

Tradition places his birth in 1582 at Sathing Phra in Songkhla, a son of Hu and Chan, bonded servants of a rich man; he was named Pu. Legend says a king cobra coiled round his cradle and left a shining crystal on his chest; a crystal said to be that one is kept at Wat Phako. A novice at fifteen and a monk at twenty, named Samiramo, he studied the scriptures in Nakhon Si Thammarat and the Abhidhamma in Ayutthaya. “Thuad” is Thai for great-grandparent: he is honoured as a revered ancestor.

Two legends tell of his journey and his learning. Sailing to Ayutthaya, when the ship’s water ran out and its owner blamed him, he lowered his foot into the sea and the water round it turned sweet. At court, envoys from Lanka brought the Abhidhamma as loose golden letters to be set in order; he found seven missing and named them, sang vi dha pu ka ya pa, the syllables that stand for its seven books, and won a royal title, but declined the king’s other rewards. Together they paint a learned monk, unmoved by reward and kind to those who wronged him.

Old royal records kept at Wat Phako tell of a senior monk, believed to be him, who restored the temple with royal support about 1610. By tradition he died in Kedah, now in Malaysia, about 1682, his ashes in a stupa at Pattani’s Wat Chang Hai. Its abbot, Ajahn Tim Dhammadharo (not Luang Phu Tim of Wat Lahanrai), identified the stupa as his and in 1954 made the first amulets of him, to fund a new ordination hall. No likeness from his lifetime is known, and much of his story was first printed in the 1950s.

Popular belief adds more. It is told that he ended a plague in Ayutthaya with blessed water, and that one night he vanished from Wat Phako with a novice, two lights circling the temple, then drifting south. Devotees honour him as a bodhisatta, some as the future Buddha Maitreya, and believe he still comes in dreams and visions; the figure on the first amulets, and their name, are said to have come that way. They believe his image shields its wearer from harm, and tell of guns that would not fire.

Luang Phu Tim is revered as one of the foremost masters of eastern Thailand. Once, two famous masters sent seekers to him; Luang Pho Ngoen of Wat Don Yai Hom told them, “Go to that monk. His concentration is exceedingly strong.” He initiated only a few disciples, and the Khun Paen made with his powder are known by his name. Wat Lahanrai, which he built up, keeps his relics and a golden image of him twelve metres across the lap, and remembers him every 16 October.

Luang Phu Tim was born Tim Ngamsri on 16 June 1879, in the reign of King Chulalongkorn, at Ban Hua Thung Ta But in Tambon Lahan, Rayong, the second of three sons of a farming family. As a young man he hunted to feed his family and served over four years as a conscript in Bangkok. In 1906 he was ordained at Wat Lahanrai as Issariko, and studied the manuals of the old protective arts left there by its founder, Luang Phu Sang Thao — his grandfather, by the temple’s 1975 book; some later accounts say his uncle.

After three years on thudong and rains retreats at Wat Na Matum in Chonburi, learning from monks and lay masters, he returned to Wat Lahanrai, studied insight meditation under several teachers, and became its abbot. For some fifty years he ate one meal a day and no meat; his room held only a bed, an old mat and a pillow. He spoke little and smiled at visitors, and every night, even when ill, he chanted and meditated from midnight until four or five. Made a Phra Khru in 1935 and Phra Khru Phawanaphirat in 1964, he told no one.

Phong Prai Kuman means “spirit-child powder”: accounts of its making describe the remains of an unborn child who died with its mother, ground with yantra-inscribed chalk and sacred plants. A book for his 96th birthday in 1975 says he made it over ten years earlier, by the mid-1960s; in the early 1970s it went into Khun Paen amulets for donors to his new ordination hall. By 1975 he had stopped; the book reports him saying: “Back then I was eager to try what I had learned. Now I want none of it.” He died that October, aged 96.

Later devotees explain the powder as an act of compassion: the spirits of the untimely dead, invited to share in merit rather than wander, are said to dwell in the Khun Paen and guard their wearers, bringing charm and goodwill (metta mahaniyom) and turning danger aside. It is told that fire flared in the mortar as the powder was pounded, and only he could quench it; that cameras would not work on him without his leave; and that he was seen on alms round in Chonburi while he stayed at his temple.

Somdej Toh is one of the most revered monks in Thai history — perhaps the most famous and widely loved of nineteenth-century Thailand. Mentor to the future King Mongkut, he rose to Somdet, the highest title a monk can hold below the Supreme Patriarch. His likeness sits in temples across the land, devotees still pay homage to it at Wat Rakhang and Wat Intharawihan, and the Chinabanchon linked to his name is among Thailand’s most popular protective chants.

Somdej Toh was born in 1788, in the first years of Bangkok under King Rama I — by most accounts at Tha Ruea, in Ayutthaya province, though his earliest biography says Bangkok. Tradition says his father was royal — Rama I or Rama II, depending on the telling — but no record proves it. A novice at about twelve and a monk at about twenty, he became deeply learned in the scriptures and trained in meditation, yet under King Rama III he is said to have refused high monastic rank, slipping away on wandering (thudong) journeys.

King Mongkut — taught by him as a boy novice, his earliest biography says — made him abbot of Wat Rakhang in 1852 and Somdet Phra Phutthachan in 1864. The biography tells how, asked in a sermon where anger arises, he feigned sleep and goaded his questioner into hurling a spittoon at him, then explained that it arises when the senses meet what displeases, but overpowers only a fool who lets mindfulness slip. At Wat Saket’s charnel ground he wrote: “Do not flaunt your courage before ghosts, nor your pride before death.”

His Phra Somdej amulets are small tablets of white shell lime and blessed powders — by tradition 84,000, the number of the sections of the Dhamma. He raised giant Buddhas: reclining at Wat Sa Tue, seated at Wat Ket Chaiyo, standing at Wat Intharawihan. The Chinabanchon chant linked to his name places the Buddha on the chanter’s head, the Dhamma in the eyes and the Sangha in the chest. He died on 22 June 1872, aged 84 — by most accounts at Wat Intharawihan, its standing Buddha only navel-high.

It is told that he sat at dusk by the grave of Mae Nak, perhaps Thailand’s most famous ghost, called up her spirit and wore a yantra-inscribed piece of her forehead bone at his waist, and her haunting died down. Another tale has a tiger watching over him all night where he lay across its path. Devotees believe his tablets guard against accidents, sickness, sorcery and ghosts, and that the Chinabanchon shields those who chant it regularly; pilgrims still collect holy water from his well at Wat Intharawihan, trusting it to keep evil spirits away.

Luang Pu Mun is revered as the Great Teacher of the Thai Forest Tradition and father of its meditation monks; his biography’s translator calls him “a towering figure in contemporary Thai Buddhism”. His disciples, among them Ajahn Maha Bua, his pupil from 1942 until the master died in 1949, carried his way across Thailand, and the tradition has now spread to several countries abroad. A museum at Wat Pa Sutthawat keeps his robes and alms bowl.

Mun was born on 20 January 1870 into the Kaenkaew family, rice farmers of Ban Kham Bong, a village in Ubon Ratchathani, in Thailand’s northeast. A novice at fifteen, he went home two years later at his father’s request. On 12 June 1893, in Ubon, he was ordained a monk with the name Bhuridatto, which Thai tradition explains as “one who gives wisdom”, and trained under the meditation master Ajahn Sao Kantasilo of Wat Liap.

With Ajahn Sao, then mostly alone, he kept the strict dhutanga life: rag robes, one meal a day from the alms bowl, nights in forests, caves and cemeteries. For decades he roamed Isan, Laos, central Thailand and Burma, then spent some eleven years in the mountains of the north. Charms, he told the people of Nong Phue, are “external things”; the amulets that bear his image were made by others. When hill villagers asked him for a spell against ghosts, his biography tells, he gave them “Buddho, Dhammo, Sangho” to repeat silently: a meditation, not a spell.

The mind, he taught, echoing the Buddha, is radiant by nature; defilements are passing visitors, like clouds drifting across the sun. He wrote very little; his teaching lives on in the monks he trained. Gravely ill at Ban Nong Phue, he asked to be carried to Sakon Nakhon town: in a village with no market, he said, animals would be slaughtered to feed the crowds at his funeral. He died at Wat Pa Sutthawat on 11 November 1949, aged 79. In 2020 UNESCO joined in marking his 150th birth anniversary.

Devotees tell of wonders. Ajahn Maha Bua’s biography of him tells that devas came at night to hear him teach, and that a naga chief from beneath a mountain near Luang Prabang came almost nightly. Monks living with him believed he read their minds: a thought at night might draw a lecture the next morning. When he wondered how monks practised in the Buddha’s day, the book tells, a Buddha or an arahant appeared in his meditation and showed him. His disciples hold that he was himself an arahant, fully awakened; devotees believe his cremated bones became crystal-like relics.

Luang Pu Phiboon is counted among the prides of Udon Thani, widely known as a monk who built up his community, a saintly monk and a famous master. The district named for him opens its motto with him, “Luang Pu Phiboon, a name renowned far and wide”, and holds a festival of homage to him each December. Wat Phra Thaen, the temple he founded, is filled with images and murals of him, among them a statue some 25 metres tall.

Luang Pu Phiboon was born Phiboon Sae Tan at Ban Phra Chao, in Roi Et province, the son of Sa, a Chinese trader who had settled there, and Sopha, a Roi Et woman. No record of his birth date survives; some writers place it in the reign of King Mongkut. A prosperous man, remembered for giving, keeping the precepts and loving-kindness, he and his wife raised an adopted daughter. When she married, he handed everything he owned to her and her husband and, with his wife’s consent, became a monk.

He crossed the Mekong to meditate in the caves of Laos, trained there for years under a teacher, then returned to Isan. Around 1900 he came to an abandoned temple site in Udon Thani whose laterite Buddha pedestal stood without an image, and named his temple for it: Wat Phra Thaen, “temple of the holy pedestal”. He persuaded the villagers to move beside it, laid out Ban Daeng’s roads, and set up rice and buffalo banks for the poor. Devotees tell of crocodiles he sent away, and of a staff left for him by a stranger.

His temple’s record recalls his teaching: give up drink and gambling, keep the precepts, chant morning and evening, and take refuge in the Triple Gem, not in spirit shrines. But state and Sangha officials, wary of Isan’s “holy man” revolts and of the old Lao-style customs he kept, detained him more than once. From about 1931 he was held at Wat Phothisomphon in Udon Thani, where he died in 1946; no revolt was ever proved against him. Phibun Rak, a minor district from 1992 and a full one from 1997, bears his name.

Popular belief credits him with great powers. It is told that officials sank him in the sea off Ko Si Chang for seven days, and that he was drawn up alive, his robes dry. Villagers said they saw him rise in meditation to the ceiling of the ordination hall, and lift a golden boat from a pond to show them, then set it back. Devotees believe he turned French bombs away from Udon’s homes into Nong Prachak lake, where none exploded; many say that on holy days a light rises from his stupa to a bodhi tree and returns.
